title: Programming Concepts and Big Data
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter is Unit 5 of Stat 243, and it comes in two parts that share a slot in the syllabus across different years rather than a single subject. The first and larger part is a tour of programming concepts — text processing, talking to the operating system, packages, types, the object-oriented and functional paradigms, memory, and efficiency — illustrated mostly in Python, with R held up next to it whenever the contrast is instructive. The second part, taught in a later offering of the course under the same unit number, is an introduction to working with data too large to hold comfortably in memory: MapReduce and Dask, relational databases and SQL, and newer columnar storage formats. The two parts do not depend on each other, but both assume you already know your way around the shell and basic regular expressions (Unit 2 and Unit 3 of the course), and basic Python or R syntax. The recurring theme of the first part is a question the instructor poses directly: *why is the language built the way it is?* Not just what a feature does, but what principle motivated it, so that the answer transfers to the next language you learn. The second part's recurring theme is more practical: once a dataset stops fitting in memory, what changes, and which of the tools you already have (the shell, `pandas`) still work and which don't. ## Part I: Programming concepts ### Why look under the hood of a language Scripting languages such as Python, R, and Julia let you interact with the operating system, call out to compiled code, and organize code into modules and packages. The concepts in this unit are illustrated mostly in Python, but they recur — implemented differently — in essentially every other language. Understanding why Python does something one way, rather than simply memorizing that it does, is what lets you evaluate an unfamiliar language quickly: what principles did its designers choose, and what did they trade off to get them? ### Text manipulation and regular expressions Python's `re` module provides Perl-style regular expressions (R's `stringr`/base `grep`/`gsub` family and the shell's `grep`/`sed` cover the same ground, evolved from the same UNIX ancestry). A `str` in this context means any sequence of characters — numbers, whitespace, special characters — not the narrower sense the word sometimes has in a given language. **Finding matches.** `re.search` returns a match object (or `None`) that you can query for the matched text, its span, and its start/end position: ```python text = "Here's my number: 919-543-3300." m = re.search(r"\d+", text) m.group(); m.start(); m.end(); m.span() ``` `re.search` only finds the first match; `re.findall` returns all of them, and `re.finditer` returns a *lazy* iterator over matches — useful when scanning a large text object, since it only computes the next match when asked, the same idea as `pandas.read_csv(chunksize=n)`. Flags such as `re.IGNORECASE` and `re.MULTILINE` change how the engine matches. A pattern can be pre-compiled with `re.compile` — this is done implicitly if you don't do it yourself, but doing it explicitly is worthwhile for a pattern reused many times, and is a reminder that a regular expression is its own small language, compiled into a finite-state machine that does the matching. **Groups, and what `findall` returns when they're present.** Parentheses group a sub-pattern, and also decide what a match "captures": ```python text = "At the site http://www.ibm.com. Some other text. ftp://ibm.com" re.findall(r"(http|ftp):\/\/", text) # returns only the captured group: ['http', 'ftp'] re.findall(r"((http|ftp):\/\/)", text) # add an outer group to capture the whole pattern re.findall(r"((?:http|ftp):\/\/)", text) # or mark the inner group non-capturing with ?: ``` Captured groups can also be referenced during a *substitution*, which is why they're sometimes called capturing groups — `\1`, `\2`, ... refer back to them: ```python text = "Here's my number: 919-543-3300." re.sub(r"([0-9]+)", r"_\1_", text) # bracket each run of digits re.sub(r"([^\",]),", r"\1", '"H4NY07011","ACKERMAN, GARY L.","H","$13,242",,,') # drop stray commas ``` The comma example works because `[^",]` matches a character that is neither a quote nor a comma; the pattern is "such a character followed by a comma", and the character is saved into `\1` so the substitution can put it back without the comma. **Greedy matching.** By default, a repetition operator (`+`, `*`, `{m,n}`) matches as much as it can. This is usually what you want (`\d+` on `"998"` matches all three digits, not just one), but it can misfire: ```python text = "Do an internship in place of one course." re.sub("<.*>", "", text) # greedy: eats everything from the first < to the last > re.sub("<.*?>", "", text) # a trailing ? makes the repetition "lazy" (non-greedy) ``` **Escaping and the backslash plague.** A backslash introduces both regex metacharacters (`\d`, `\w`) and Python string escapes (`\n`, `\t`), and since Python 3.12 a regex like `\d` inside an ordinary string literal is no longer silently passed through — it must be written `\\d` (or, more cleanly, as a *raw* string, `r"\d"`, which turns off Python's own escaping and leaves the regex engine's escaping as the only kind in play). Searching for a literal backslash is the extreme case: you need two backslashes as the regular expression (to match one literal backslash), and to write those two backslashes in an ordinary string literal you must escape each of them — four backslashes in the source to find one backslash in the text. A raw string cuts this in half: `r"\\"` matches one backslash. R hits the same wall for the same reason (`\.` is "not a recognized escape" in R; `grep("\\.", x)` is required), and the shell needs fewer backslashes than either, since it has only one layer of quoting to fight through rather than two. ### Talking to the operating system and to compiled code **The filesystem and the shell.** Both Python and R let you shell out and capture the result: ```python import subprocess files = subprocess.run(["ls", "-al"], capture_output=True) files.stdout ``` ```r files <- system("ls", intern = TRUE) ``` Both languages also provide direct, OS-portable queries — `os.path.exists`, `os.listdir`, `os.path.join` in Python; `file.exists`, `list.files`, `file.path` in R — and information about the running system (`platform.system()`, `os.uname()`, `Sys.info()`). Writing paths with `os.path.join` / `file.path` rather than pasting `/` or `\` by hand is what makes code *agnostic* to the underlying operating system. `options()` in R (width, digits, max.print) controls how much and how precisely R prints to the screen — useful to know, and a trap if you compare two `digits`-rounded numbers on screen and expect `==` to agree with what you saw. A script can be made directly executable: give it a shebang line (`#!/usr/bin/env python` or `#!/usr/bin/env Rscript`), `chmod +x` it, and run it as `./script.py`. Command-line arguments arrive via `argparse` in Python or `commandArgs(TRUE)` in R, and in both cases it's your job to interpret the incoming strings as the numbers or booleans you actually wanted. `Ctrl-C` interrupts execution and generally unwinds gracefully back to where you started — except when the interpreter is thrashing against a memory limit, in which case the interrupt itself can take a long time to take effect, which is exactly when you most want it to be quick. **Calling out to compiled code.** Scripting languages call out to C, C++, Fortran, or Java because they are themselves often much slower than compiled code — a language like Julia, which JIT-compiles its own code, needs this less. R's ancestor language, 'S', was built at Bell Labs specifically as an *interactive wrapper around Fortran*, the dominant numerical language of the era, and that heritage still shows: R's `.Call` interface and, more usably, the `Rcpp` package let you write C++ that reads almost like R and pass data back and forth easily. Python calls C directly via the extension API, or, more conveniently, via *Cython*, which can translate typed Python to C and let you define callable-from-Python C functions. ### Modules, packages, and namespaces A large add-on ecosystem is part of why a scripting language becomes popular, and the causality runs both ways: Python's numerical core (`numpy`, `scipy`) is itself a package, distributed via PyPI and Conda. A package must be *installed* once (`pip install` / `conda install`) and then *imported* in every session that uses it (a few, like `os` and `re`, ship installed by default but still need importing). A *module* is a `.py` file of functions, classes, and variables; `import mymod` binds the name `mymod` in the current namespace to that module's own namespace, so `mymod.x` and a bare `x` in your session are genuinely different objects unless you go out of your way to merge them with `from mymod import x` (usually avoided, since it risks silent name collisions and reduces modularity — if two modules both define `x` and you `from`-import both, whichever import ran last wins, quietly). A *package* is a directory of modules plus an `__init__.py` that runs on import and can re-export names so users don't need to know the internal module layout — this is how `numpy.linspace` is reachable directly even though it lives in `numpy/core/function_base.py`. Names prefixed with `_` are a convention for "internal, please don't import me directly"; Python does not enforce this the way encapsulation is enforced elsewhere, it only makes `from pkg import *` skip such names. Subpackages nest this structure further, and can be auto-imported by the parent's `__init__.py` (relative import, `from . import subpkg`) or left for the user to import explicitly (absolute import, `import pkg.subpkg`, resolved via `sys.path`). **Installing and reproducing an environment.** Dependencies are usually resolved automatically by `pip` or `conda`; `mamba` is a faster drop-in replacement for `conda`'s dependency resolution, and the `conda-forge` channel is the usual source of up-to-date community packages. `pip freeze` / `conda env export --no-builds` capture exactly which packages and versions you're using, into a file that recreates the environment elsewhere — the `--no-builds` flag strips system-specific build details that wouldn't transfer to a different OS. A Conda *environment* (`conda create -n myenv python=3.13`) gives you a fully independent Python executable and package set, isolated from whatever else is on the machine. A *source* package ships raw code (Python, and any C/C++/Fortran it wraps) as text, compiled on your machine when installed — this needs a working compiler but produces code tuned to your system. A *binary* package (a Python *wheel*, for instance) ships already-compiled code, needing no compiler but tied to the platform it was built for. *Building* a pure-Python package is a no-op (nothing to compile); *installing* just means placing it somewhere Python will find it — `sys.path` shows where, and a package's own `__file__` and `__version__` attributes show exactly where a given copy came from, useful when you suspect two different installed versions are shadowing each other. **The same landscape in R.** R's packages live on CRAN; the convention is to call them *packages*, not *libraries* — a *library* is the directory where packages are stored. `library()` loads a package (or, with no arguments, lists everything installed); `.libPaths()` shows where R looks, and `searchpaths()` shows where currently-loaded packages actually came from. A package's objects live in their own namespace, invisible to `ls()` until the package is attached; `search()` lists the currently attached namespaces in lookup order. Installing "from source" versus from a pre-built binary is the same source/binary distinction as in Python, and needs the same developer tools (Xcode, Rtools) when a package contains compiled code. ### Types, data structures, and coercion **Static versus dynamic typing.** A *type* determines how a value is stored and what can be done with it. Compiled languages such as C require every variable's type to be declared in advance — *static* typing. Python and R are *dynamically* typed: a name can be rebound to a value of a different type at any time, with no declaration: ```python x = 'hello'; x = 7; x = {'mykey': 7} ``` Dynamic typing is convenient for fast, exploratory work and avoids friction from small type mismatches. Static typing costs that convenience but buys two things back: it catches a class of input errors before the program runs at all, and it lets the runtime skip a check-the-type step on every operation, which is a real part of why compiled code is faster. **Types in Python and numpy.** Beyond the built-in scalars (int, float, string, bool) and containers (list, tuple, dict), `numpy` supplies array types for numerical work. numpy will sometimes *widen* a type to make an operation work — an array built from `[3, 5, 7.3]` becomes an array of floats — which is usually convenient but occasionally not what you meant, so numpy also lets you force a type explicitly with `dtype=`. This distinction matters concretely on a GPU, where 32-bit floats are the default rather than the 64-bit ("double") default elsewhere. **Mutability.** Lists, dicts, numpy arrays, and R's ordinary vectors can be modified *in place*. Tuples, strings, and sets in Python cannot — attempting `x[1] = 4` on a tuple raises an error. This distinction resurfaces later, in the discussion of pass-by-reference: only mutable objects can be changed from inside a function in a way that's visible outside it. **Coercion.** Converting between types — casting — happens explicitly (`str(x)`, `int(x)`) or implicitly, and the two languages differ in how forgiving they are about the implicit kind. Python raises an error assigning the string `'hat'` into a numeric numpy array; R happily coerces the whole vector to character instead. Indexing with a non-integer is another divergence: Python raises an error on `myList[2.73]`, while R's `x[2.73]` truncates to `x[2]` without complaint. Neither behavior is simply "right" — the tolerant one hides more bugs, the strict one demands more discipline of the caller. **Dataframes and split-apply-combine.** `pandas` picked the dataframe concept up from R, and `dplyr` and `pandas` both implement the *split-apply-combine* pattern for stratified analysis: split a dataset by one or more grouping variables, do something to each subset, combine the results. This pattern is not particular to statistics — it is essentially the same shape as a standard SQL query (`GROUP BY` plus an aggregate), and it is essentially the same shape as *MapReduce*, the framework underlying big-data tools such as Hadoop and Spark (Part II returns to this). R's tidyverse packages layer *non-standard evaluation* on top of this — writing `group_by(country)` rather than `data$country` — which reads nicely at the console but complicates writing a function that takes a grouping variable as an ordinary argument, since the variable name itself, not its value, is what's being captured. **Object protocols.** Python groups objects into broad categories — `mapping`, `number`, `sequence`, `iterator` — called object protocols, each with a defined interface (a `sequence` has a length and ordered access by index; an `iterator` has a notion of "next" and of "stopping"). A class you write can participate in a protocol by implementing the right set of dunder methods, taken up next. ### Two paradigms: functional and object-oriented programming *Functional programming* (FP) centers on functions: modular, ideally side-effect-free, taking inputs and returning outputs, treatable as black boxes, and themselves passable as ordinary values (as `map` does). *Object-oriented programming* (OOP) centers on objects belonging to classes: a class defines *fields* (data) and *methods* (functions bound to that data), and calling a method can change the object's fields. A useful statistical analogy: an object is to its class as a realization is to a random variable. Where FP is organized around *verbs* — a computation is a sequence of function calls — OOP is organized around *nouns*: a computation is a sequence of operations on persistent objects. Both R and Python are multi-paradigm, but R leans functional and Python leans object-oriented. Which style fits a given problem often follows from its shape: a data-analysis pipeline that transforms data step by step reads naturally as function composition; a simulation that tracks the internal state of, say, a `Student` object (register, assign a grade) reads naturally as OOP. ### Object-oriented programming **A worked example: simulating a time series.** The class below stores the parameters of a correlated Gaussian process and can produce independent realizations from it (a squared-exponential correlation, $\mathrm{Cor}(t_i, t_j) = \exp(-(t_i - t_j)^2 / \text{cor\_param}^2)$, with the realization generated as $\text{mean} + U^\top z$ for $z \sim N(0, I)$ and $U$ the Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix): ```python class tsSimClass: def __init__(self, times, mean=0, cor_param=1, seed=1): self.n = len(times) # public self.mean = mean self.cor_param = cor_param self._times = times # private (by convention) self._current_U = False self._calc_mats() np.random.seed(seed) def set_times(self, new_times): # setter: keeps the object consistent self._times = new_times self._current_U = False self._calc_mats() def simulate(self): if not self._current_U: self._calc_mats() return self.mean + np.dot(self.U.T, np.random.normal(size=self.n)) def _calc_mats(self): # private: caches the expensive part lag_mat = np.abs(self._times[:, np.newaxis] - self._times) cor_mat = np.exp(-lag_mat**2 / self.cor_param**2) self.U = np.linalg.cholesky(cor_mat) self._current_U = True ``` `times` is deliberately private, reached only through `set_times`, because the correlation matrix and its Cholesky factor are both functions of `times`: letting a user overwrite `times` directly would leave the object internally inconsistent, and hiding it behind a setter also lets the class control *when* the expensive Cholesky factorization is redone rather than redoing it on every call to `simulate`. This is *encapsulation*: shielding internal state from direct modification so the object can enforce its own invariants. Python does not truly enforce privacy — a leading underscore is a convention the caller can ignore — but the convention itself, and the design reason behind it, is the point. **Copies and references.** Plain assignment does not copy an object: ```python myts_ref = myts # same object, two names myts_full_copy = copy.deepcopy(myts) # genuinely separate object myts.set_times(np.arange(1, 1001, 10)) myts_ref.get_times()[0:4] # changed along with myts myts_full_copy.get_times()[0:4] # unaffected ``` A deep copy is safer — a caller can't accidentally mutate your object through an alias they don't know they share — but it costs the time and memory of actually duplicating the data. This tension between reference semantics (cheap, but shareable) and copy semantics (safe, but costly) recurs through the rest of the unit. **Inheritance and polymorphism.** A class can be built on another, adding fields and methods: ```python class Bear: def __init__(self, name, age): self.name, self.age = name, age def color(self): return "unknown" class GrizzlyBear(Bear): def __init__(self, name, age, num_people_killed=0): super().__init__(name, age) self.num_people_killed = num_people_killed def color(self): return "brown" ``` `GrizzlyBear` inherits `Bear`'s constructor logic via `super().__init__`, adds a field, and *overrides* `color`; Python looks for a method on the specific class first and falls back to the base class only if it isn't found there. `statsmodels`' `OLS` inheriting from `WLS` is the same idea put to statistical use. This is *polymorphism*: the same method name (`color`) behaves differently depending on which class the object actually belongs to, and an instance of `GrizzlyBear` is polymorphic in that it can be treated as either a `GrizzlyBear` or, more generally, a `Bear`. *Abstraction* — hiding how a method does its work behind a fixed interface — is what lets you change `_calc_mats`'s internals later without breaking any code that only ever calls `simulate()`. A class attribute (shared across all instances, like a running count of how many `Bear`s have been created) is distinct from an instance attribute (`name`, `age`, private to one object) — and, disconcertingly, Python lets you bind a brand-new attribute onto an existing instance or even a function object at any time, which is legal but rarely a good idea. **Generic-function OOP and dunder methods.** `len(x)` "just works" on a list, a numpy array, or a dict because Python doesn't special-case each type inside `len` itself — it calls `x.__len__()`, whatever class `x` happens to be. This is *generic-function* dispatch, and the alternative — a giant `if`/`elif` inside `len` checking every possible type — would be worse in three ways: someone has to write and maintain that branching logic; it all lives in one function regardless of how many cases there are; and, most importantly, a user's own new class could never plug in, because they don't control the `len` builtin. Generic dispatch makes the system *extensible*: any class that defines `__len__` automatically works with `len`. *Dunder* ("double underscore") methods are the mechanism: `__init__` (constructor), `__str__` (what `print` shows), `__repr__` (what typing the object's name shows), `__len__` (what `len` calls), `__add__` (what `+` calls), `__call__` (invoking the object like a function), `__getitem__` (subscripting). Objects are, under the hood, dictionaries mapping attribute names to values or methods, and dunder methods are what let a class hook into Python's built-in syntax and functions. The dispatch that `len` and `+` use only looks at the *first* argument. Julia's *multiple dispatch* chooses a method based on the types of several arguments at once — genuinely useful for mathematical code, where an operation's efficient implementation can depend on the types of both operands. R's older S4 system, and its newer R7 system, both support multiple dispatch as well. **Object protocols: iterators and context managers.** A container that supports `for x in obj` implements `__iter__` and `__next__`. Tuples are iterable containers but are not themselves iterators — you can loop over a tuple repeatedly precisely because iterating doesn't consume it; `zip(...)`, by contrast, produces an iterator that *is* consumed as you call `next` on it. The `with` statement is sugar over exception-safe cleanup: ```python with open('myfile.txt', 'r') as file: lines = file.readlines() ``` is equivalent to a `try`/`finally` that guarantees `file.close()` runs regardless of what happens inside the block. Any class can participate by defining `__enter__` and `__exit__` — the *context manager protocol* — invoked automatically on entering and leaving the block. A database connection that must always be closed, opened via `__enter__` and closed via `__exit__`, is the natural real-world use. **R's three approaches to OOP.** R does not have a single object system; it has (at least) three, of increasing formality. *S3* is deliberately informal: an S3 object is simply a list (or other primitive object) with a `class` attribute attached, and dispatch works through `UseMethod`, which looks at an object's class and calls the matching `.` function (falling back to `.default` if none exists). `lm` and `glm` are the standard example — a `glm` object's class is `c("glm", "lm")`, so `summary.glm` is tried first and `summary.lm` second. Because there is no formal class definition, nothing stops you from reassigning `class(obj)` to something nonsensical; the informality that makes S3 easy also makes it unchecked. *S4* is stricter: `setClass` declares named, typed *slots* (accessed with `@`, not `$`), and a `setValidity` function can enforce invariants (an age between 0 and 130, say) every time an object is constructed or modified — though only through the constructor and explicit validity checks, not automatically on every slot assignment, so a user can still set `sam@age <- 150` and bypass the check. S4 supports multiple dispatch (`setMethod` on a signature naming more than one class) and, via `setClassUnion`, something like an interface shared across otherwise-unrelated classes. *R6* (and the older, slower Reference Classes) departs from both by giving R genuine pass-by-reference objects: fields declared `public` and `private`, methods that mutate `self`/ `private` state in place, and — crucially for the discussion of copying above — assignment does *not* copy an R6 object: ```r mytsRef <- myts # same object; changes to myts show up in mytsRef mytsFullCopy <- myts$clone() # myts$clone() is the deep copy ``` which is the same reference-versus-copy distinction seen in the Python version of this same example, now made explicit with a `clone()` method rather than a `copy.deepcopy` call. R6's private fields are enforced at the language level (assigning directly to a private field raises "cannot add bindings to a locked environment"), unlike Python's underscore convention. ### Functional programming, scope, and closures **No side effects, and how R and Python differ on it.** A function with no side effects only produces output through its return value — nothing about the caller's environment changes just from having called it. This matters because it lets you treat any function as a black box: you never need to read its body to know whether it might quietly rebind one of your variables. R's functions are, in this sense, closer to the ideal, because R passes arguments *by value*: ```r myfun <- function(x) { x[2] <- 7; return(x) } x <- 1:3 new_x <- myfun(x) x # unmodified — myfun operated on a local copy ``` Python passes *by reference*, so the same pattern silently mutates the caller's object unless you are careful: ```python def myfun(x): x[1] = 7 return x x = np.array([1, 2, 3]) new_x = myfun(x) x # modified! ``` Avoiding this requires an explicit copy inside the function (`y = x.copy(); y[1] = 7; return y`). Even R breaks its own rule where it must — `par()`, `library()`, `plot()` all have side effects by necessity. **Functions as first-class objects.** Everything in Python — including functions and classes — is an object that a name can be bound to, the same way `x = 3` binds a name to an integer: ```python x = sum x([1, 3, 5]) # 9 — x is now callable ``` A function can be looked up by name (`getattr(np, "mean")`), passed into another function as an ordinary argument, and returned from a function. A function that takes or returns another function is a *higher-order function* — `map` is the canonical example. **Map operations.** A *map* applies a function to every element of a collection: ```python list(map(abs, [1.0, -2.7, 3.5, -5.1])) [pow(val, 2) for val in [1, 2, 3]] # list comprehension: also a map ``` A *lambda* is a function defined inline and never given a name (`lambda vals: vals * 2`); `functools.partial` pre-fills some of a function's arguments, producing a new function (`partial(round, ndigits=3)`). Map-style code (`subsets.apply(analysis_function)`) is usually shorter and clearer than the equivalent explicit loop, and map is also the conceptual core of *MapReduce*, which Part II covers for genuinely large data. **The call stack.** Running code produces a nested series of function calls — the *call stack* — which grows (is *pushed*) each time a function calls another, and shrinks (is *popped*) each time one returns, like a stack of cafeteria trays. Python's error messages show the whole stack, which is thorough but can be verbose; R shows only the innermost frame by default, with the full stack available via `traceback()` on request. Understanding this ordering is what makes an error traceback readable rather than an undifferentiated wall of text. **Function arguments and outputs.** Arguments without defaults must be listed first in a definition, and must be supplied by the caller — by position, or by name (`add(z=-5, x=3, y=5)`), but positional arguments must precede keyword ones. `*args` collects any number of extra positional arguments into a tuple; `**kwargs` does the same for keyword arguments into a dict. `os.path.join(*x)` unpacking a list into positional arguments is a common use. `return` can appear anywhere and exits immediately; returning several values (`return x, res`) packages them into a tuple; a function called only for its side effects can omit `return` entirely, which is equivalent to `return None`. **Pass by value versus pass by reference, generally.** Pass-by-value copies each argument, so changes inside the function never escape it — safe and modular, at the cost of the time and memory of copying. Pass-by-reference passes enough information to find and modify the original object — efficient, but harder to reason about, since a function's effects are no longer visible just from its return value. Numpy arrays and other mutable Python objects are pass-by-reference (tuples, being immutable, can't be modified this way regardless). The rule that decides which case you're in: if the function *rebinds* the parameter name to a new object, the caller's object is untouched; if it *mutates part of* the existing object (`f_x[0] = 99`), the caller sees the change, because `f_x` and the caller's name were referring to the same object all along. This is the same mechanism as a C pointer: passing a pointer copies only the address, and code that dereferences it can modify the original data in place. **Namespaces and the LEGB rule.** A *namespace* maps names to objects; a *scope* determines which namespaces are visible from a given point in the code, and scopes nest. Python resolves an unqualified name by searching, in order: **L**ocal (inside the current function), **E**nclosing (any function this one is nested inside), **G**lobal (the module), **B**uilt-ins. Crucially, the *enclosing* scope is the scope where a function was **defined**, not where it happens to be called from — this is *lexical scoping*, shared with R and most other languages, and it is what makes the following resolvable at all rather than ambiguous: ```python y = 100 def fun_constructor(): y = 10 def g(x): return x + y # looks up y in the enclosing (fun_constructor) scope, not the caller's return g myfun = fun_constructor() myfun(3) # 13, using y = 10, even though fun_constructor has already returned ``` `global` and `nonlocal` let a function reach out and assign into the global or an enclosing scope respectively (R's equivalent is `<<-`); doing so is occasionally useful but makes a function harder to reason about as a black box, for the same reason side effects generally do. **Closures.** A *closure* is what makes the example above work at all: `fun_constructor` returns `g`, and `g` keeps access to the enclosing namespace (containing `y = 10`) even after `fun_constructor` itself has finished executing and would otherwise be gone. This gives you something like a minimal, single-purpose OOP object built from functions alone — data bound directly to a function, and protected from outside interference in a way a bare global variable would not be: ```python def scaler_constructor(data): def g(param): return param * data return g scaler = scaler_constructor(x) del x # no longer needed — the closure still has its own reference to it scaler(3) ``` Closures generalize to *function factories* that stamp out a family of related functions from one constructor (a `number_formatter('US')` versus `number_formatter('EU')` closure, each remembering its own `notation`), and to stateful accumulators (a `make_container(n)` closure that fills a preallocated array one call at a time, useful for something like collecting bootstrap means without either a global variable or a full class). **Decorators.** A decorator wraps a function to extend its behavior without editing its body: ```python def verbosity_wrapper(myfun): def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): print(f"Starting {myfun.__name__}.") output = myfun(*args, **kwargs) print(f"Finishing {myfun.__name__}.") return output return wrapper @verbosity_wrapper def myfun(x): return x ``` The `@decorator` syntax is sugar for `myfun = decorator(myfun)`. Real uses include timing a function automatically, counting how many times it's been called, setting up a task to run in parallel under `dask` (Part II), or, via `jax.jit`, compiling a function just-in-time — see the efficiency section below. ### Memory and copies **Two facts to hold onto.** A numeric array element is 8 bytes (a 64-bit float, or "double"); and the central bookkeeping question when reasoning about memory is *when is a genuinely new copy of an object created*, versus when is a new name simply bound to an existing one. **The heap and the stack.** The *heap* is where objects created while a program runs actually live; it grows as needed and the interpreter's garbage collector reclaims it. The *stack* holds the local variables of each active function call — one frame per call — which is why the sequence of active calls is called the *call stack* or *stack trace*. **Allocating and freeing.** Unlike C, Python and R never require you to allocate or free memory explicitly — the interpreter tracks references and reclaims memory once nothing points to an object any more (*garbage collection*). `del x` in Python (`rm(x)` in R) does not itself free memory; it only removes the name, and the interpreter cleans up the now-unreferenced object shortly after. Forcing collection (`gc.collect()` in Python, `gc()` in R) is rarely needed and costs time when called. **Monitoring memory use.** `top` or `free -h --si` (Linux/Mac) show overall system memory: the `buff/cache` column is memory the OS is using to cache disk reads, which is immediately reclaimable and so should be counted as available, not used — `available` is roughly `free` plus `buff/cache`. *Swap* is disk pretending to be memory when physical memory runs out; heavy swap use means a job has slowed to a crawl and should be treated as a warning sign, not tolerated. Inside Python, `psutil` reports the current process's memory use, and `sys.getsizeof(x)` reports the size of a single object — but naively, since an object that merely *contains a reference* to a large object reports only the size of the reference, not the referenced data (`sys.getsizeof([3, x])` badly underestimates the size of a list holding a large array `x`). A reliable trick when the naive size is misleading: serialize the object (`pickle.dumps`) and check the length of the byte string, since serialization has to actually write out everything the object refers to. **`id`, `is`, and how copies show up.** `id(x)` gives the memory address behind a name; `is` tests whether two names refer to the *same* object (as opposed to `==`, which tests equality of value). Assignment (`y = x`) makes `id(x) == id(y)` and `x is y` true — no data was copied, only a new name was bound to the existing object. `x.copy()` makes a genuinely new object with its own id. Applying `id` across the elements of a Python list shows that the list itself is essentially an array of references: two elements can point at the very same underlying object (`obj[0] is obj[1]` can be `True`), and one list's element can share memory with part of an entirely different object. Numpy arrays behave differently: because they need contiguous storage for fast vectorized arithmetic and linear algebra, an individual element is not its own addressable Python object — `x[1]` manufactures a brand-new scalar object each time it's evaluated, so calling `id` on it twice in a row gives two different addresses, unlike a list. One consequence: pickling a numpy array gives a size barely above the raw byte count of its numbers, while pickling an equivalent list is more than double that size, reflecting the pointer overhead of storing each element as its own Python object. **Modifying in place versus copying.** Changing an element of an existing numpy array (`x[2] = 3.5`) leaves `id(x)` unchanged — no copy is made, which is exactly what you'd want, since copying on every element assignment would make working with large arrays impossibly slow. A *shallow* copy (`x.copy()` on a list) makes a new top-level container but leaves nested objects shared; mutating a nested list still shows up in both copies. A *deep* copy (`copy.deepcopy`) recursively duplicates everything, leaving nothing shared. **When are copies actually made, and how does the interpreter know it can free memory?** Rebinding a name to a brand-new object (`x = np.random.normal(size=10**8)` a second time) uses new memory only because a genuinely new object was created — the old one becomes unreferenced and is eventually collected. Python tracks *reference counts*: `sys.getrefcount(x)` reports how many names currently point at `x` (the count is always one higher than expected, because passing `x` into `getrefcount` itself creates a momentary extra reference), and once the count reaches zero the memory is reclaimed. The same idea — reference counting to decide when a copy is unavoidable — appears in C++ shared pointers, and in R. **R does the same bookkeeping under a different name: copy-on-modify.** R keeps a reference count per object (visible via `.Internal(inspect())` or `pryr::refs()`/`pryr::address()`) and only actually copies an object at the moment it is modified *while more than one name refers to it*: ```r a <- rnorm(5) b <- a # a and b share one object; refs(a) is now 2 a[2] <- 0 # only now, because b also points at it, is a's object copied ``` If you instead modify an object referenced by only one name, no copy happens — the address is unchanged. This is the same underlying question ("does anything else still need the old value?") that Python's reference counting answers directly at assignment time; R defers the decision to the moment of modification instead, which is why it's called *copy-on-modify* rather than copy-on-assignment. (Versions of R before 4.0 implemented this with a coarser `NAMED` flag that could be fooled into copying when it wasn't necessary, or occasionally into *not* copying when it was — the modern reference-count scheme is more reliable.) Lists and character vectors get the same treatment: only the specific components that change are copied, not the whole structure — this became true only as of R 3.1.0, before which modifying one element of a list copied the entire list. **Strategies for saving memory.** Avoid unnecessary copies; delete objects you're done with so the garbage collector can reclaim them; prefer iterators and generators to materializing long lists you're only going to loop over once; use a narrower numeric type (`float32`, `int16`) when the precision or range you actually need allows it; read large files in chunks rather than all at once (Part II); and consider a columnar in-memory format such as Arrow when memory efficiency really matters. **Worked example: `fastcount`.** This function — real code from a PhD student's research, shown here in its Python translation — is worth reading specifically for *where it allocates memory*: ```python def fastcount(xvar, yvar): naline = np.isnan(xvar) naline[np.isnan(yvar)] = True localx = xvar.copy() localy = yvar.copy() localx[naline] = 0 localy[naline] = 0 useline = ~naline # ... ``` `np.isnan(xvar)` allocates a new boolean array the size of `xvar`; `.copy()` is called explicitly (and deliberately) on `xvar` and `yvar` so that zeroing out the `NaN` positions doesn't mutate the caller's original arrays; `~naline` allocates yet another same-sized array. If `xvar` and `yvar` are each very large, this one function call is quietly responsible for several arrays' worth of temporary memory, all of it necessary for correctness (not mutating the caller's data) but easy to underestimate by reading only the "logic" of the function and not its allocations. ### Efficiency: lookup, caching, and just-in-time compilation *A gap in the source material*: the notes for this section open mid-way through a discussion of vectorizing an operation on a matrix `D` with special structure (the setup — what `D` is and why combining it with another matrix `X` the direct way is slow — is missing from the converted lecture notes). What survives is the second half of the efficiency discussion: lookup cost, hashing, cache-aware programming, loop fusion, and just-in-time compilation. One incomplete prompt from the missing part survives as a **Tip** in the notes: for a matrix `D` with exploitable structure and an ordinary matrix `X`, how would you compute $X + D$, $DX$, or $XD$ by vectorized operations rather than the naive translation of the mathematical expression? More generally: a sparse or otherwise structured matrix (e.g. block-diagonal) can be worked with far more efficiently than treating it as an arbitrary dense matrix — `scipy.sparse` is the usual Python entry point. **Lookup speed and hashing.** Indexing into a list by position and looking a key up in a dictionary turn out to run at essentially the same speed in Python, both **$O(1)$** — constant time regardless of how large the collection is — while looking a value up by scanning a list of labels for a match is **$O(n)$**, and measurably slower once `n` is not tiny. The mechanism behind the constant-time dictionary lookup is *hashing*: a hash function maps a key (of arbitrary size) to a fixed-size output deterministically — the same key always hashes to the same value, and even a tiny change to the input changes the output (this is also what makes a git commit hash, or a file checksum, useful as a fingerprint). Taking the hash modulo the table size gives a bucket index directly, without scanning anything: ``` hash = hashfunc(key) index = hash % array_size ``` Collisions — different keys landing in the same bucket — are unavoidable once the output is a fixed size, but with a good hash function each bucket holds only a handful of entries, and a short linear scan within one small bucket is still effectively constant time overall, because it doesn't grow with the number of key-value pairs stored. R, by contrast, does *not* hash when looking values up by name in a named vector or list — it scans linearly — so name-based lookup in R is markedly slower than index-based lookup, unlike Python's dictionaries or R's own environments (which are hash-based). **Cache-aware programming.** Beyond main memory (RAM), a processor has small, very fast caches (L1 smallest/fastest, through L3 largest/slowest), and keeping the data actually being worked on inside the cache — a *cache hit* — is much faster than fetching it from main memory on every access (a *cache miss*). Memory is read from RAM into cache in contiguous chunks, so operating on values that are stored next to each other is faster than operating on values scattered through memory. Numpy arrays are, by default, stored in *row-major* ("C") order, so summing along a row reads contiguous memory and summing down a column does not (unless the array is small enough to fit entirely in cache) — the effect is visible when the summation is written as an explicit loop over rows or columns, though when `np.sum(..., axis=...)` is used instead, numpy's own implementation appears to already handle the access pattern well enough that the row-versus-column difference in the lecture's timing largely disappears. This kind of consideration matters most when writing low-level (e.g. C) code directly, but the row/column effect is visible even from Python when it's not hidden behind a library that has already optimized for it. **Loop fusion and JIT compilation.** A vectorized expression like `np.exp(x) + 3*np.sin(x)` allocates a full-size temporary array for `np.exp(x)`, another for `np.sin(x)`, another for `3*np.sin(x)`, and finally the sum — several arrays' worth of memory and several passes over the data, where a single hand-written loop computing `exp(x[i]) + 3*sin(x[i])` element by element would need no extra memory and only one pass. Combining separate vectorized operations into a single pass like this is called *loop fusion*; Julia does this automatically as a compiler optimization, and it is also a key optimization performed by *XLA*, the compiler behind JAX and TensorFlow — which is one route to getting fusion-like performance from Python. JAX behaves like a GPU- (and multi-core-CPU-) aware numpy, and can *just-in-time (JIT) compile* a function to machine code via XLA. A demo on the course's compute cluster comparing a numpy version of `np.exp(x) + 3*np.sin(x)` against a JAX version, on an array of $5 \times 10^8$ elements, showed: | version | time | | --- | --- | | numpy | 17.181 s | | JAX (not JIT-compiled, running on CPU threads) | 5.722 s | | JAX, JIT-compiled (`jax.jit`) | 3.218 s | — roughly a 3x speedup from JAX's parallelism alone, and a further 2x from JIT compilation on top of that, consistent with the compiler having fused the separate `exp`/`sin`/multiply/add operations into one pass. `jax.jit` can be applied either as a plain function call (`jax.jit(myfun_jnp)`) or, more often, as a decorator (`@jax.jit`) — tying this back to the decorator mechanism above. **Lazy evaluation.** This R snippet looks wrong until you notice what's *not* being timed: ```r f <- function(x) print("hi") system.time(f(mean(rnorm(1000000)))) ``` `rnorm(1000000)` is passed as an argument to `f`, but `f` never uses `x` at all — and R never actually evaluates the expensive argument, because R evaluates function arguments *lazily*, only when (and if) they're actually needed inside the function body. The general idea — delaying computation until it's genuinely required, so that a whole pipeline of steps can potentially be optimized jointly rather than run one at a time — recurs well beyond R: in TensorFlow's original (graph-building) execution model, and, centrally for Part II, in Dask and Spark, both of which build up a description of the computation and only actually run it when a result is explicitly requested. Python itself, notably, does not have lazy evaluation of function arguments. ## Part II: Working with big data ### What "big" means, and what it doesn't buy you "Big data" as a buzzword has faded somewhat, but the underlying fact hasn't: the current wave of AI/ML is built on the availability (and scrapability) of enormous datasets. Some of the hype is justified — a large dataset lets you address questions a small one can't, and supports more sophisticated (e.g. nonlinear) models — but size on its own solves none of the classical problems of inference. A dataset with medical records for every American still doesn't establish that salt intake *causes* hypertension; that requires either a designed experiment or careful reasoning about observational data, and no amount of additional rows changes that. An ad hoc "sample" — internet transaction logs, say — is not a statistical sample, however large, and does not license inference about a population the way a properly drawn sample does; the difficulty of drawing reliable conclusions about Covid despite enormous quantities of data is a case in point, because the data were incomplete and non-representative rather than merely small. A large dataset can, at least, enable a *large number* of analyses and tests, which raises its own problem: with enough analyses run, something will look interesting by chance alone, with no underlying reality behind it — a documented issue in analyses of electronic health records specifically, a common data source for health research. What "big" means, concretely, also depends on who's asking: sometimes it's about literal size (and speed of collection), and this course's usage is comparatively modest — datasets that are large by the standards of typical statistical work (gigabytes to tens of gigabytes) but nowhere near what Google or the NSA would call large. Sometimes "big data" instead describes how pervasive data-backed analysis has become in society, independent of any one dataset's size. **The concrete limitation.** Both Python and R keep all objects in memory, so you cannot directly work with a dataset larger than roughly 1–20 GB, depending on the machine. The tools in this unit target the gigabytes-to-tens-of-gigabytes range (further if the machine has abundant memory, or if you're willing to trade time for disk space); beyond hundreds of gigabytes or into terabytes, you want a properly administered database, a cloud platform (AWS, GCP), or Spark. It also matters where the data physically sits: keeping it on the local disk of the machine doing the computing avoids the delays of moving it over a network. **What you already know is often enough.** UNIX commands are fast, and manipulating data through shell piping — `grep`, `head`, `tail`, `awk` to filter rows, extracting specific columns — can shrink a dataset to something manageable before it ever needs to be loaded. GNU parallel lets you parallelize shell operations, and is commonly used on Linux clusters. And simple discipline goes a long way: drop columns you don't need before loading the rest; a random sample of a large dataset may answer your question as well as the full dataset would; a binary storage format is usually more compact than a flat text format like CSV; and for many purposes, simply putting the data in a standard database (below) already solves the problem. ### MapReduce and Dask **Why MapReduce.** Traditional high-performance computing focused on message-passing (MPI) between processes running an efficient shared algorithm. The last two decades have added a different paradigm aimed specifically at datasets too large for one machine: distribute the data (and ideally the computation) across many machines, and let them appear to the user as a single dataset. *MapReduce* is the basic pattern: - read individual records (lines of a CSV, individual files, ...); - **map**: transform each record into a key-value pair (a record can also be dropped, or expanded into several records, at this step); - **reduce**: for each key, aggregate across all the values assigned to it; - write out the resulting (key, result) pairs. The constraint that makes this parallelizable is that each record is processed independently in the map step, and each key is processed independently in the reduce step. This is recognizably the same shape as `pandas`/`dplyr`'s split-apply-combine (Part I), and Python's own `map` function is the same idea at a much smaller scale. The one operation to be wary of is anything requiring a *shuffle* — moving a lot of data between workers to complete an aggregation. Computing a group mean or sum is cheap, because each worker can compute its own partial sum and the partial sums are simply added; computing a group *median* is not, because it genuinely requires seeing every value in the group together, wherever it happens to live. *Hadoop* is infrastructure that implements MapReduce across a cluster: its distributed filesystem (HDFS) stores data redundantly across machines, computation runs where the relevant data already sits (minimizing network traffic), and failed tasks are automatically retried on other nodes. *Spark* can be thought of as Hadoop with the pooled memory of the cluster treated as one large in-memory workspace, which makes it faster than Hadoop whenever the working data fits in that combined memory (falling back to HDFS when it doesn't); it's more approachable than raw Hadoop but still nontrivial to configure well, and failures — often memory-related — can be hard for a user to debug. **Dask.** Dask parallelizes across the cores of one machine or across a cluster, processing a dataset in *chunks* (also called partitions or shards). Two practical benefits follow directly: computation (including reading from disk) happens in parallel across workers, and because each worker only ever holds its own chunk, a dataset can be processed with far less memory per machine than its total size would suggest — though reading many chunks from a single physical disk in parallel is itself limited by that disk's own throughput, which is why Hadoop/Spark clusters typically spread data across one disk per node. Dask provides three main collection types, mirroring three familiar Python structures: - **Dask dataframes** are Pandas-like, made of many smaller Pandas dataframes stacked by row. Handled by the `threads` scheduler by default. Loading an 11 GB flight-delay dataset and then computing, say, the mean departure delay for a particular carrier and origin airport looks like ordinary `pandas` code with an added `.compute()` at the end — because Dask evaluates *lazily*: reading the files, filtering, and grouping are all only actually executed once `.compute()` is called, and calling `.compute()` twice re-reads and re-computes everything from scratch, which is why a real pipeline should chain all its operations before the single call to `.compute()` that triggers them. (`.compute()` on a large enough result also silently pulls the *entire* thing back into one ordinary, non-distributed, in-memory Python object — worth checking the expected size of before you call it.) Dask, notably, will not compute an exact median on a dataframe column — the reason follows directly from the shuffle discussion above. - **Dask bags** are like Python lists but explicitly unordered (asking for "the 5th element" isn't meaningful), handled by the `processes` scheduler by default, and support parallel `map`-style operations — filtering a large collection of raw Wikipedia log lines for ones matching a regex, for instance, or converting each line into a tuple and then into a Dask dataframe for further structured analysis. - **Dask arrays** are numpy-like, chunked along both axes into smaller numpy arrays, handled by the `threads` scheduler by default. Because chunks are generated on demand rather than materialized all at once, an 80 GB Dask array can be processed using only a few GB of actual memory. Whether chunking primarily by row or primarily by column matters for a row-wise reduction (like a row mean) turned out, in the lecture's own timing, to make little practical difference — plausibly because the reduction itself needs only a small amount of data (the running partial sums) moved between workers, regardless of how the chunks are laid out. ### Databases and SQL A relational database is a collection of tables (*relations*) — much like R or `pandas` dataframes — where each table's columns (*fields*/*attributes*) have a single type, and rows are individual records. Tables sharing a field are joined together to combine information across them. Formally, a database lives on disk while Python/R objects live in memory, which would suggest databases are slower — but disk caching by the operating system, plus algorithms built specifically for fast querying and joining, often make a database perform competitively. Interacting with a database means talking to a *DBMS* (database management system) — SQLite, DuckDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and others — via *SQL*, the Structured Query Language (with DBMS-specific variations). SQLite and DuckDB are both single-file, serverless databases, convenient for one-machine work; DuckDB stores data *column-wise* rather than row-wise, which speeds up analytical queries that scan large portions of a few columns (so-called OLAP workloads), and can query data on disk without pulling all of it into memory first. **Normalization, motivated by a bad schema.** Suppose a school's data — students, teachers, classes, enrollments and grades — is put into one giant table, one row per student, with columns `class_1`, `class_2`, ..., `class_n` and matching `teacher_name_1`, `teacher_age_1`, and so on. This has several real problems: information is repeated across rows (every student of a given teacher repeats that teacher's age, wasting space and, worse, requiring the same fact to be updated in many places at once if it changes); students taking fewer than `n` classes leave many cells empty; and the table has to commit in advance to a maximum `n`, which breaks the moment one student exceeds it. *Normalizing* the schema — spreading the data across linked tables so no fact is stored twice — avoids all of this: A table's *primary key* uniquely identifies each row (`Student.ID`; for `Enrollment`, the pair `{student_ID, class_ID}`, since neither alone is unique); a *foreign key* is a column in one table holding the primary key value of a row in another, and a join matches rows by equating a foreign key in one table with the primary key it refers to: ```sql SELECT Student.ID, grade FROM Student, Enrollment WHERE Student.ID = Enrollment.student_ID AND Student.grade_level = 9; ``` (It's possible to be too pure about this — if every query ends up rejoining the same set of tables anyway, a deliberately *denormalized* schema, or a saved *view* that behaves like a virtual table built from a query, can be the more practical choice.) **The anatomy of a query.** SQL is *declarative* — you state what result you want, and the DBMS's query optimizer decides how to compute it — as opposed to an *imperative* language, where you specify the exact sequence of steps. The standard shape is ``` SELECT FROM WHERE ORDER BY ``` with `WHERE` filtering rows and `ORDER BY` (computationally the most expensive clause, and often omitted) sorting them. `GROUP BY `, paired with an aggregate such as `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` in the `SELECT` list, is SQL's version of split-apply-combine — filtering *after* grouping requires `HAVING` rather than `WHERE`, since `WHERE` is applied before the grouping happens. `DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows (or duplicate values of a single column). **Joins, more precisely.** An *inner join* keeps only rows that match in both tables — a question with no answers, or (hypothetically) an answer with no question, would simply not appear. A *left outer join* keeps every row from the first table, filling in with nulls wherever the second table has no match (so a question with zero answers would still appear, paired with a null answer); a *right outer join* is the mirror image, and a *full outer join* keeps unmatched rows from both sides. A *cross join* pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, with no matching condition at all — usually not what you want, since its size is the product of the two tables' row counts, but it is the operation an inner join reduces to once you add the matching condition back: ```sql select * from table1 join table2 on table1.id = table2.id; -- explicit inner join select * from table1, table2 where table1.id = table2.id; -- same result, implicit syntax select * from table1 cross join table2 where table1.id = table2.id; -- same result, via cross join select * from table1 join table2 using(id); -- same result, shorthand ``` **Indexes.** An index orders a table's rows by one or more fields specifically so the DBMS can find matching rows without scanning every row in sequence. Without an index, a lookup is **$O(n)$** — linear in the number of rows; a tree-based index brings this to **$O(\log n)$**, useful for range conditions (`viewcount > 10000`); a hash-based index brings exact-match lookups to **$O(1)$**, at the cost of being useless for a range query. Creating an index itself takes time (worth it only if you'll run enough queries against that column to amortize the cost), but a well-chosen index can turn a many-second query into a sub-second one. **Beyond single joins.** `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, and `EXCEPT` apply ordinary set operations to two query results with matching schemas — sometimes a cleaner way to express something that could, with more effort, be written as a join. A *subquery* — a complete query nested inside a `FROM` or `WHERE` clause of another — lets you build up a complicated query in stages (find the users who ever posted a question tagged 'python', then compute something about only those users) without first materializing an intermediate view; for a genuinely large database, submitting the whole thing as one query, rather than two, also gives the optimizer the chance to plan across the entire computation at once. ### Recent storage formats and sparsity Rather than a formal database, large datasets increasingly live as a collection of files — often in *Parquet* or plain CSV — sometimes called a *data lake* when this sits in the cloud. *Apache Arrow* (via `PyArrow` in Python, or the `arrow` package in R) is an efficient in-memory columnar representation: values within a column are stored contiguously, so that any single value can be retrieved in **$O(1)$** without reading the rest of the column, and Arrow reads from disk only as much as a given computation actually needs, rather than loading an entire file up front. *Polars* is a `pandas` alternative built on the Arrow columnar format, advertised for speed, and — like Dask and Spark — evaluates lazily, which lets it optimize a whole query rather than one operation at a time. Many statistical methods produce or rely on *sparse* matrices — the neighborhood/conditional- dependence structure of a graph, the structure implied by an autoregressive model over time or space, or the sparse parameter and covariance estimates produced by the lasso in high-dimensional regression, among others. A sparse representation stores only the nonzero entries and skips any arithmetic that would only ever multiply by a zero, which is both a memory saving and (often the larger win) a computational one; Python, R, and MATLAB all provide sparse-matrix types for exactly this reason. ## Exercises These are the instructor's own questions, embedded in the lecture material as prompts rather than a formal problem set; none are answered in the source. 1.
